title: Does growth follow the contractor?
question: For contractors with five or more measurable agreements, is the share that grew by a quarter or more above the rate for the same kind of work and department, by more than chance would give?
finding: 12 contractors have five or more agreements with a first and latest ceiling in the Board's files (42 more have three or four). Across all 622 measured agreements 49% grew by a quarter or more and 56% of those with dates ran a year or more long. None of the 12 sits above the rate for its own kind of work and department at the one-in-twenty level; about 0.6 would be expected to by chance alone. A second test on the 364 agreements whose contractor has at least one other: the contractor's other agreements predict growth worse than the department and kind of work do (average squared error 0.232 against 0.216; 0.251 knowing neither). On this evidence growth in Board-approved agreements goes with the department and the kind of service more than with the contractor; construction, where the question matters most, is barely in these files. For construction, the commission records added since give a direct test. Of 43 builder-and-department pairs with five or more construction contracts, 3 needed commission-approved price increases more often than their department's rate at the one-in-twenty level, where about 2.1 would by chance (Sierra Mountain Construction Inc, 6 of 14 at Public Utilities Commission; Pilot Construction Management Inc, 3 of 12 at Airport; Mitchell Engineering, 4 of 8 at Public Utilities Commission); a builder's other contracts predict a rise of a quarter or more worse than its department does. After such a rise 43% of builders were awarded new construction contracts by the same department, against 50% of those that closed out near the original. So, plainly: on the records now on disk, overruns on construction do not follow particular builders beyond what chance and the department explain; they follow the department, the kind of contract and the job. The test is weak for small builders, and individual change orders are still not public.
how: Board of Supervisors titles from 2014 to 2026 were linked into one record per agreement, following only links proven by a dollar figure carried from one title to the next or by a shared contract number (the rule used in the amendment-growth screen). The first amount is the total in the first approval on file or, where the first file is an amendment, the amount that amendment says it started from; the latest is the highest total approved. Left out: 527 leases and property; 225 no usable name in the title; 167 agreements with other public bodies; 164 no amount in any title; 58 loans; 21 agreements that bring money in (concessions, rents, franchises). For each contractor: agreements measured, how many grew by a quarter or more, the median rise among those that grew, the rise in all its ceilings together, and the share that ran a year or more past the first end date. The expected share is the rate among other contractors' agreements for the same kind of work in the same department (the kind of work citywide where fewer than eight such agreements exist), leaving the contractor's own out. "Chance" is the probability of at least that many growing if each agreement grew at its expected rate. The second test predicts each agreement twice, once from the expected rate and once from the share of the same contractor's other agreements that grew, and compares the errors.
limits: Five agreements is a small number: a contractor would need nearly all of them to grow to stand out, so this test can miss a real difference. Every agreement here reached the Board, most because they were amended, so the rates are high for everyone. Nearly all contractors with five or more are nonprofits running health and shelter programmes, whose agreements are extended as a matter of course. The rate that would answer the question for builders, change orders against the bid on each construction contract by contractor, is kept by departments and is not in any file read here. Amounts, parties and dates taken from Board file titles are read by machine: in a hand check of 50 titles, 11 had at least one field read wrongly (4 after later fixes).
